projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Sobonya was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran John Sobonya. Mr. Sobonya served in the U.S. Army with Special Services. He served in the China Burma Indian Theater and his highest rank was T3. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Sobonya's home in Solden, Ohio, on September 15, 2005. John was 87 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: In 1941, I was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were already in the Army?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: I was one of the first ones -- first group that was drafted in 1940, November of 1940. One of the national lottery numbers, you know, so the first group to go in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you won?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: So we went.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where did you go for basic training?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: I was inducted in November and we were sent to Fort Thomas in Kentucky and then we spent a few days there. And then we were sent to Fort Custard for basic training up in Michigan. Fort Custard, Michigan. And after our basic training there, I was transferred to Fort Hayes in Columbus, Ohio. I was there till November of '42. And when Pearl Harbor was attacked, I was due to be discharged from the Army the Thursday after Pearl Harbor. Pearl Harbor came up, so they told us we're in the Army for the duration. So we were in -- so we were in there. So I spent another year at Fort Hayes and then I was transferred to Fort Benning, Georgia, and I was there about a year. And then we were transferred to Pittsburgh -- Fort Pittsburgh in California. And then we were shipped out to -- our first stop was Shillong in India. We shipped from San Francisco. Then we spent like 35 days on the water. One of the cute things happened on our way, we were on the water about 28 or 29 days and we reached Australia and somebody spotted a land. And this was a big boat. We had like -- they tell me anywhere from four to eight thousand people. So I don't know exactly how many people exactly, but we had a lot. So when they spotted this land, somebody says "land." So everybody came out and got off to one side and we shifted the cargo and we sailed into Australia with a tilt -- tilted ship, tilted at an angle. So they told us all to go on the other side of the ship until they rearranged the cargo again. So we stood there for hours and hours before we got the ship sailing at an even keel. Then we went to Shillong. We spent some time there at a British camp. And then after that -- the time we spent in the British camp -- we went to Bombay, India. And there we were reassigned to go to Ramgarh, India, which we never heard of. We didn't know where it was. So it was the Har (ph) Province, India, and then we spent a couple of -- some time there in India. And we were basically treating -- training the Chinese in the use of guns and mortars. And also a training camp for drivers, for Chinese drivers to learn how to drive the American trucks. So we spent some time there on that. And they were clothed and they were outfitted completely with ammunition and guns and so to go into the Burma and then into China. At that time, the Japanese were in control of China and they were coming to take over India and they thought Burma was going to be an easy target. But it -- it turned out to be a real tough target for them. So if Burma would have fell, it means India would have also fallen. But fortunately they stopped them in Burma and then, of course, we stopped them in China. So I was discharged in November of 1945 at Fort Harrison in Indiana.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to a particular outfit when you went overseas?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: I was in Special Services. Now that meant that we had this lend-lease administration. And that meant you had to make sure the Chinese were getting all the equipment for this lend-lease. So that was our job, to take care of the Chinese, really, rather than the Americans. So when the Chinese came in for training, it was all up to us to make sure they were comfortable and they had everything they needed. So that was Special Services.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you attached to the Army or the Army Air Corps?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: I was attached to the Army at that time. And we didn't have no designation as a unit at that time. So we're just there at Ramgarh. So I didn't know what it was -- what the unit -- it might have been on this book we looked at, but I don't know. They never gave us a designation of what unit we were. We were a special unit training the Chinese.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was your specific job that you did?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: My specific job was we would -- at the PX -- we had to take care of the PX. And we had a kid that took care of the theaters and anything pertaining -- setting up boxing matches and we had a rodeo also. And the Indians didn't like how we handled the cows and the horses, you know, in the rodeo. And they weren't too happy about that. We put on a boxing match for just the Chinese alone. And the interesting part of that was that we had to give two medals. The Chinese had a custom you can't lose face. So we had to give a medal to the loser and a medal to the winner, a trophy to each one of them, you know. It was one of the things we did. And then we also took care of our local people, our GIs. One thing that stands out in my mind is we were getting all these cigar and cigarettes and Coke syrup. Of course, the cigars and cigarettes and the candy we could -- we knew what to do with. But when the syrup came in, we had nothing to do with it. Couldn't mix it; no machinery. And then we had a taxi cab driver, Larry Hoffman, out of Boston and a fella called Lou Glazer. He was an attorney. And the two of them set up this unit to make Coke. And they had a production set up. It took them about six months. And they went out and got these bottles and caps for the bottles. And then they got -- we paid some of these local Hindus and Indian people to help us with those. And after about six months, they got a production line going. And, of course, we sold the Coke for a nickel a bottle just to keep our heads above water. So I thought that was a nice little vignette.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did it taste like Coke?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Oh, absolutely. Really good Coke. I mean the British gave us a big hand, too, you know, getting the bottles and the caps. And they had these special caps that you had to put the handle down on the stamping thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: It worked out real good. So that's just one of the things that -- one of the things I thought you might like.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now you said you worked with the theater. So did you work with the USO shows when they came to town?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Right. That was -- that was our job to take care of them. To house -- to billet -- find billet for them and to feed them and take care of them and move them around from different places to different units. So we did that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did they perform basically just in that area?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah. We had just our area there around Ramgarh. And some of the stars were Paula Goddard and Joey Brown, that I can think of. Dick Gordon and a few more stars from Hollywood at that time. Andre Castellanas was there. Lily Ponds was one of them also. Then we had a few more that I can't think of right now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a chance to talk to any of them?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I had to give -- Keenan Wynn at that time was a big star in Hollywood at that time. I had a motorcycle and that was my means of transportation to and from my billets to the Special Services job. So he came in for this weekend and treated us to entertainment and he borrowed my motorcycle. It wasn't borrowed; I was ordered to give him my motorcycle while I was there. So he was a motorcycle fan, so he took my motorcycle for a weekend. But I didn't mind that because they were real nice to us. So that's some of the few things I remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you stationed in Ramgarh the whole time?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: No. I was there two years at Ramgarh. Then I went to --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The whole time you were overseas though?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah. Two years in Ramgarh and spent almost a year in China -- Kunming. I was in China.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Was that when the war was still going on or was that after?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: That was during the war. And then that year the first -- they dropped the atomic bomb, the first one. And this -- I think this was like in May or something like that. The first atomic bomb -- then, of course, we didn't know what an atomic bomb was. We called it an electronic bomb. We didn't know what it was. And then when they dropped the second bomb in China --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Japan?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Japan rather. Then I knew that the world might be coming to an end. And, of course, that was it. September they surrendered, and I was there a little while longer. And then I was shipped out of Kunming the last week of November in China and then we went to Calcutta. We flew to Calcutta and then we came across a victory ship in the Suez Canal, United States. And that's where I was discharged, Fort Harrison.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what do you remember about life when you were living in India? First Ramgarh. What was life like there?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Well, where we were at, we had it very good. Because we were on what they call per diem. We had to buy our own food. We didn't get food like the rest of the people did, C-rations and K-rations. So we had to go out and get our own food. And I was one of the buyers. So all along, people trying to bribe me with all kinds of stuff, potatoes and stuff, and they were trying to bribe me to give them their business. In the meantime, people were checking on us to be sure we spent the money properly. So that was one of the things I had to do. That was very interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would they monitor you to be sure you weren't taking bribes or --

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Well, they told us to be very careful, because you're being watched when you handle that kind of money. To go out and buy stuff for the PX, they were -- we didn't know who they were or where they were. We never knew. But they warned us, don't do anything shady. Be sure you're getting our money's worth, account for every penny. So that was part of our job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the food okay?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: The food was very good. Of course, we got some food -- we ate water buffalo quite a bit. And a few times we had lamb from Australia. And also, I think, we had one or two shipments of beef from Australia there at one time. But we were doing good at getting our own connections. The British were a big help to us. You know, they know where to go and what everything cost. So they helped us a lot. Those are a few of the things I can remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did Ramgarh ever come under attack of any sort from the air maybe or --

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: No, no. We had no attacks. We had no attacks and Ramgarh was just a little -- little place. I would say maybe a few hundred, three hundred, four hundred people. And Ranchi was the closest place, a little bigger town. And we went there for entertainment and so on. Change of pace. Ranchi, India. And the only transportation was if we went by trucks. They would take us down like 5 or 6 o'clock in the afternoon and pick us up at 9 o'clock in the evening. So if you missed your truck, you're out of luck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in China when you were there?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: China was a little bit tougher. When we got there, our water -- we had water, but you couldn't drink it. We had to go to the kitchen and drink the kitchen water. But we were taking showers in the water. They told us not to get any in our mouth. It was a little bit on the rusty side. Then after we were there about two or three months, it was all cleared up. Then we had nice, good, clean showering water, and we had good drinking water, kitchen only. You drank all your water -- you were allowed -- first time we were there, we were allowed like a canteen full of water for one day. But it was changed later, and you could get all you wanted when they got the pure water in. And one of the vignettes is that we had a big cemetery behind us, and they would bring food for the dead people. That was one of their customs, you know, traditions. And one of the GIs asked him, when are they going to eat the food that you put here? He said, well, they're going to smell your flowers first and then their gonna come eat the food. So I thought that was kind of a cute reply.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Let's see, I had a question there and it kind of slipped my mind. Oh, I know the answer to this question, but I'm going to ask for the purpose of the tape. Did you do any souvenir collecting over there?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yes, I did. I did quite a bit, especially in India. I got a lot of stuff. Not too much in China; not too much in China.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is this mostly stuff you were able to purchase from the local people?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh, local people. Of course, we went on furloughs a few times and we picked up items there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Including two large, nice knives from the Gurkhas.

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why don't you explain a little bit about what the Gurkhas --

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: The Gurkhas were small Indian people back in the jungles and they were vicious fighters and they knew the jungle and they knew how to handle themselves in a jungle. So when the British incorporated them into their army, they went out to fight the Japanese. And the Japanese were really frightened of these Gurkhas because they were really -- knew what to do in the jungle. And so as they advanced first, we get these Gurkhas and we usually go in behind the Gurkhas after our group went in. So I thought that was kind of interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because you knew the Japanese would scatter?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah, they didn't want to come in contact with the Gurkhas. And, like I mentioned before, they were just paid their money for their duty that they did there just within the last year or two. I don't know how much money they gave them, but they were finally paid.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And this was paid by the British government?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: The British government, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you collected some jewelry and some incense burners and things like that. Were you able to send this stuff home without any problem?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: No. We had no problem whatsoever sending any of this stuff. They were -- of course, they were censoring our mail. All our mail that was sent out was censored, you know. We wrote the letter and then the officer would censor and then it would go forward. What it was, I understand, they were getting our letters and they were using them on microfilm. And they were reprinting them again when they got to this country. And they would reenlarge them again, and that's how our folks got messages. But for awhile there, all our mail was censored by the officers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much mail or packages from the States when you were over there?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: No packages. No. We got mail, but I can't remember ever seeing a package overseas, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would have been a long haul?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Well, I got very friendly with my foreman.

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: foreman worked for me, and we were in charge of projects around the camp. And Hyatt Muhammad -- Hyatt was my foreman, you know. And he took care of all the translation between the workers and myself. So he was a real nice guy. When he would take me to his house, he would introduce me to his family. All the kids. But all the time we were there, he never brought out his wife. I never met his wife. But I did meet his brothers and uncles and kids. But never his wife. I never knew why. I never questioned that, of course. But that was kind of odd.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You never found out why you didn't meet her?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: No, huh-uh. Never did know. Never introduced me to his wife. Never saw --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Must be something cultural or something?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: I didn't think -- I didn't think -- could be. That was one of the things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you say you finally came home?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: I came home in November of 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Oh, gosh, everybody cried. They were happy to see me back. And they treated me royal when I got home. I mean, everybody wanted me over for dinner, wanted me to tell about what happened, my experiences. I thought that was rather nice; it was a nice welcome. Then after a few -- awhile -- after a few weeks, I started looking for a job, you know. Then I went to -- my brother-in-law and I went into the carpet laying business, so we were in that for awhile. So that was another experience. But, all in all, it was an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now that first year or so of the war, especially right after the attack of Pearl Harbor and the Japanese advanced in the Pacific, did you have any doubts that we were going to win?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: No, I didn't. But that was a real shocker when Pearl Harbor happened, because I was due to be discharged the following Thursday. As a matter of fact, I gave some of my stuff back to the GIs; I thought I was not going to need it. And then after they declared -- give it back to me again. So then they told us we're in for the duration, so forget about being discharged. Then, of course, we were at the recruiting -- down at Fort Hayes. We were -- people were coming in and we had to induct them into the Army. We had to feed them and clothe them and so on and they were there just a very short time, maybe a week or two. And then they were assigned to different units. And I was there for I don't remember how many months. But we went through a lot of outfitting. I was in the shoe department, fitting shoes for the GIs. We had a production line, you know, socks, underwear, shirts, shoes, neck ties, and equipment and all the way down the line. And I was fitting shoes all the time. So some of the sizes were -- we had sizes anywhere from size five up to, like, 12 that were standard sizes. But anything over that, we had to order special. So some of the sizes went up as high as 15. Some of the boys in the back country there had extra wide feet. So that was a few of the things we did there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to deal with the complaints if the shoes didn't fit?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Well, what they did when they came in, we measured the size. There was a bucket of sand on each side of the person. They had to reach down with two hands, one bucket with each hand, and lift it up, and that was the shoe size that registered. According to Army regulation rules, that's what we had to give them. So they'd lace it up and walk around and try it. And if they didn't fit, didn't like the feel, come back and we'll try something else. So we tried to take care of them real well, be sure that they got the proper fit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. I'm trying to figure out. They had to lift up the buckets?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Bucket of sand on each side and that way we got the proper --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because that would...

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: That would give them the weight on the base of their feet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Weight of the feet?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh. And then, of course, they had to lace it up and walk around. And then if they had any questions, then we would change up or down, whatever they wanted. Whatever would be comfortable for them. So that's the story on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I never heard that before.

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think back to that time, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind when you think about that time?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Well, nothing particular. But I know when we got in the Army, 1941, we were outfitted with the World War II equipment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: World War I, right?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Yeah, World War I. And we got the coats from World War I. We got leggings. I know everyone was issued leggings. At that time, we had wraparound leggings rather than the lace up. And we thought that was odd. And after about a year or so, everybody got equipped properly with the standard equipment. But until that point, we were receiving even some of the World War II coats. I understand that they were sewing -- they were patched, you know. But that didn't last too long. They got up to par on that. I was amazed about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it seems like we weren't really prepared for war?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: Oh, no. We didn't have enough. Sometimes we'd run out of different size shoes, you know, so we'd have to wait. And so we had to wait until the proper size came. It usually took about the two weeks before we would get the proper size.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: John Sobonya
sp.p: That's about it.
